title: On the Primacy Bias in RLVR Training
claim: Experiments control how skewed the pretrained knowledge is, and split training data into easy examples that match it and hard examples that oppose it.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, left-to-right, colorbar for skewness and shaded class regions
description: Two side-by-side line plots show the controlled toy setup for image classification. The left panel, titled 'Pre-trained distributions with different β', plots density against class index 1–10. It draws a family of curves coloured from light to dark blue by a β colorbar (0.5 to 3.0). Higher β gives a sharper decay: nearly all mass sits on class 1 and the tail is flat. A black double arrow and the note 'Higher β = sharper decay' mark this trend. The right panel, 'RL data distribution', overlays three class-density curves. D_easy (blue) decays from the dominant classes, shaded light blue at left. D_hard (red/pink) rises toward the rare classes, shaded light red at right. D_uniform (green) is a flat line at 0.1. Rotated labels read 'Aligned' and 'Misaligned'. The eye goes first to the dark blue steep curve, then to the crossing blue and red curves.
caption: Experimental designs on toy example of image classification. 1) The pre-trained data distribution is controlled by the skewness parameter β, greater skewness induces strong bias towards dominant classes. 2) The class distribution of RL training data consists of Deasy, Dhard, and Duniform. Easy examples align with pre-trained knowledge, whereas hard examples are misaligned with it and predominantly belong to rare classes.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.
